title: Fifa World Cup plans: Gianni Infantino scraps private investment proposal after widespread opposition
description: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment planImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since Febr
body: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment planImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since February 2016ByJack SkeltonBBC Sport senior journalist and Simon StoneChief football news reporterUpdated 4 hours agoFifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors following widespread opposition.Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."Infantino had offered Fifa's 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.However, Uefa - which governs European football - responded by voting to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead, and other governing bodies also voiced their opposition.On Friday, Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.It means Infantino is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March."Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve," the 56-year-old added in a statement."Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game."AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa welcomed the withdrawal of the plan."The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he said.Infantino's plans were unlikely to passDespite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".However, Infantino would have needed the backing of a majority of member associations to pass the plans - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.Governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.Conmebol - South American football's governing body - said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.What was Infantino's plan?Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".There was no mention in the document of the women's game.Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.Can Infantino survive?Figure caption, How does Fifa actually make decisions?Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman by 115 votes to 88. Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen member associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed" - but the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.Cordeiro, who represented Fifa on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at the governing body to resign over the plans.In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite"."If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."'Bruised Infantino makes humiliating climbdown' - analysisByChief football news reporterAs reports first emerged on Tuesday about Fifa's plans, a senior figure in English football told me the story would be as big, if not bigger, than the European Super League.I do not think he felt it would unravel in quite the same way - but the idea only took two days longer than Super League to be scrapped.There have been no fan protests on the streets, but animosity towards the plans was evident from the moment the likely implications dawned on the game.Infantino is an astute politician. He knew the numbers were against him and has decided to cut his losses now rather than risk further personal damage.It is a humiliating moment - but for Infantino, the real work starts now. He has some significant bridge building to do.In their statement - which, in its own way, was just as damning as Uefa's threatened boycott - the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) pointed to a much wider issue. "The AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal," it read. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."Infantino cannot just walk away from the past few days as though nothing has happened. There are a lot of angry people in football who feel he has been acting beyond his power - just as the organisation's chief operating officer suggested on Friday.The immediate crisis has passed. Over the short to medium term, it will be fascinating to see whether Infantino can restore his reputation.

title: Thousands evacuated in Crete as wildfires threaten tourist resorts
description: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firef
body: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firefighters died on the island on Wednesday when they became trapped while tackling a fire near Krya Vrysi in the Rethymno region. A third firefighter died on the Greek mainland, near the port town of Gytheio in the Peloponnese. As gusts reached 125km/h (77mph) on the island, around 8,000 people were evacuated from their homes overnight but were later allowed to return.Greece is among many European countries facing devastating fires and drought. Several fires have continued to burn in Spain and Portugal, although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared an end to the national emergency for wildfires in the Ávila and Madrid regions.In south-west France some residents have been able to return to their homes after a major wildfire in the Gironde region.The fire raging in Crete broke out in the Rethymno region on Wednesday and has since spread rapidly, destroying homes and agricultural land. It remains one of the biggest fires currently active on the island and is still burning out of control.There was no clear picture of the destruction so far, Rethymno's deputy regional governor Maria Lioni said, adding that containing the fire was the main priority.Lioni described Wednesday as a "dark day" for the region and said gusts overnight reached up to 11 on the Beaufort scale - a wind force categorised as "violent" - fanning the flames and hampering containment efforts.Some of those evacuated in Rethymno were moved into a temporary shelter."I was watching the fire and I just didn't know what to do. It was like a volcano down the side of the mountain," said Bianca Boorer, who was visiting the coastal resort of Agios Pavlos with her mother on a yoga retreat."The bar staff told us you need to get in cars and drive away but only two people had cars. Eleven people tried to get into one tiny car and the car my mum was in was nearer to the fire," she told the BBC's Your Voice."The place we had breakfast in has burnt down. Agios Pavlos hotel has burnt down, the place we did yoga in has also burnt down."Meanwhile, wildfires have erupted in the north-western Spanish provinces of Zamora and León, not far from the border with Portugal, with more than 1,000 people evacuated.Five people were injured in a fire in the eastern town of Valpaços in Portugal, according to local reports.A major fire that consumed an area in excess of 66,000 hectares to the west of the Spanish capital, Madrid, and caused tens of thousands of people to be evacuated has stopped spreading, allowing some residents to return home.As he ended the national emergency in the area, Pedro Sánchez urged "extreme caution" during the fourth heatwave of the summer in Spain.The fire in Ávila, which has burned more than 43,000 hectares over the past week, is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history. A small amount of rain fell near Bordeaux in France on Thursday, raising hopes that the Gironde wildfire that has burned an area larger than the US city of Detroit and destroyed 240 homes might soon be over.The region's fire service said it was "reasonably optimistic" given that the fire had not grown in size since the weekend.Around 84,000 of the 220,000 displaced residents were allowed to return home on Thursday, according to French reports.It is estimated that more than 90,000 hectares of land across France have burnt this year - higher than any other year on record, according to data from the European Forest Fire Information Service.In Spain, more than 200,000 hectares have burnt in 2026 – roughly five times above the average for the time of year. The area of land ravaged in Portugal is also higher than usual for this point in July.The European fire season typically extends into August and September – and with more hot weather on the way in the coming days, these figures are likely to keep rising.Most wildfires are started by humans, whether deliberately or accidentally, but climate change is strengthening weather conditions conducive to fires spreading.Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive heatwaves, generating tinder-dry fuel for wildfires.Some researchers have also warned that the Mediterranean's forests and scrublands are not being properly managed – leaving plenty of vegetation as fuel for fires.Forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected.In Turkey, hundreds of homes have also been evacuated but the majority of fires that have broken out mainly in the south have been brought under control, authorities say.If you are affected and it is safe to do so, please get in touch by using this link or the form below.

title: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura G
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura Gozzi and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorHungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said.The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it. Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week.Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer.The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania.Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment.A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Large areas of the riverbed have been exposed in the centre of Budapest after weeks of extreme heat and droughtIn Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power.The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production.Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Among the wrecks exposed by the low levels of the Danube was a World War Two German warship at Prahovo in SerbiaRomania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600cm per second. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500cm per second by Tuesday.The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries.The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea.The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia. And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth. They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib.Image source, Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik/ReutersImage caption, River flow in Serbia on the Danube is now a third of the average for JulyShipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania.  Passengers had been running low on food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, and another boat that was called in to help was unable to get close enough."I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Boats lie on the dried-out Danube riverbed in front of the Calafat-Vidin bridge, connecting Bulgaria and RomaniaIt is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube.Serbian hydrologist Dejan Vladiković said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring. He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September.Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C.Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected. Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory, leading to hundreds of thousands of evacuations.
